newsitem.title: FRANCE: No franc crisis despite French EMU debate.
newsitem.headline: No franc crisis despite French EMU debate.

text.p: Economists on Friday played down the chance of a new franc crisis despite the reopening of a debate in France on the merits of a strong franc policy and the push toward European monetary union.
The franc was on the way up at midday, trading at 3.3905 per mark at 1128 GMT, down from around 3.38 per mark on Wednesday, but up from its low on Thursday night of 3.3975.
Economists said there was certainly no franc crisis underway and they believed the unit was unlikely to fall through 3.40 per mark barring some major new development.

"International investors will be reluctant to short the franc aggressively because every time they have done that they have gotten their fingers burnt," said BIP-Dresdner economist Marie Owens-Thomsen.
"In the short term, I'd be surprised if it (the franc) fell through 3.40 per mark," Owens-Thomsen added. "With extra bad news, we might go to 3.42, but that's a minor disaster scenario."
Economists said a switch in attention to the lira, which many expect to rejoin the European Exchange Rate Mechanism this weekend, could also take pressure off the franc.
And preliminary third-quarter French gross domestic product data, due next Thursday and expected to show a healthy rise, could help revive optimism about the economy.
"In my opinion we had the worst of it yesterday. It's not a crisis so far," said Jean-Louis Mourier, economist at Louis Dreyfus Finance.
"As long as we are talking about fluctuations within the old ERM (European Exchange Rate Mechanism) bands, you cannot call it a crisis," Owens-Thomsen said.

Several factors combined in recent days to give the franc trouble, including a tough truckers' strike, weak economic data, market rumours of a cabinet reshuffle and the dollar's drop to under 1.50 marks.
But a call on Wednesday by former president Valery Giscard d'Estaing for a franc depreciation that reopened a debate in France on the merits of European monetary union was the trigger.

Mourier said Giscard's remarks were given greater weight by a joint statement from Prime Minister Alain Juppe and German Chancellor Helmut Kohl on Thursday saying the franc-mark rate was in line with economic fundamentals.
The statement also strongly reaffirmed their countries' commitment to EMU.
"That was taken pretty badly by the markets because it added weight. A lot of people said Giscard had little influence. It gave added importance to his (Giscard's) views," he said.
Immediately following the statement, the franc slipped nearly half a centime.
But economists said it was important not to forget the impact of a weakening dollar on France's economy and warned that a lower U.S. currency could seriously hurt the franc.
"There must be a risk that it will go a bit lower, but the greatest risk to the franc was not these comments, it's the fall of the dollar," Owens-Thomsen said.
The dollar weakened in recent days due to a huge U.S. trade gap and signs the U.S. eocnomy was slowing.
The German economy's apparent acceleration was also doing little good.
ABN Amro economist Philippe Brossard said the "Giscard effect" accounted for around one centime of the franc's fall with the rest due to dollar's weakness.
He saw any further slide in the franc coming to a halt around 3.4050 per mark.
